issues.description: The manuscript states that CREP required and all included studies collected a minimum N of 120, yet the reported replication sample sizes include 80, 81, 90, 90, 94, and 116. This contradiction affects evaluation of inclusion criteria, power, and whether studies actually met the stated CREP requirements.
issues.quote: "All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)"; "Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374."

issues.description: The individual replication studies were small for detecting the focal effects, especially effects around r = .15 to .22. Several replications had N around 80–90, making nonsignificant results difficult to interpret. The claim that N = 120 ensured adequate power is unsupported by any power analysis and contradicted by actual Ns below 120.
issues.quote: "The CREP team specified the minimum sample size required for the replication; this size was generally set at the original study’s sample size"; "Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374."

issues.subcategory: unaccounted excluded or incomplete replication attempts
issues.description: The OSF project had 17 forks but only seven studies were included. The manuscript does not account for the remaining ten forks, whether any collected data, why they failed to meet criteria, or whether exclusion could bias the meta-analysis. This is a serious completeness and potential selection-bias problem for a replication meta-analysis.
issues.quote: "The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 ‘forks’ representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process"; "These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository."

issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that missing-data handling, exclusions, composite calculations, and item-level data were not consistently documented. This prevents verification of analyses and could materially affect correlations, reliability estimates, and meta-analytic inputs.
issues.quote: "not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc. Data were not always collected or stored consistently"

issues.description: Some studies lacked analysis scripts and some lacked item-level data. This makes the stated open-data/open-materials status less sufficient for reproducibility because key analytic decisions cannot be reconstructed for all included studies.
issues.quote: "Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed."

issues.description: The studies are described as direct replications, but they differed in administration mode, setting, group versus individual testing, item wording, item order, and response scale. These variations can influence self-report responses and reduce interpretability of pooled results as direct replications of the same procedure.
issues.quote: "researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods)"; "the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six"; "one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items"; "two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale."

issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether participants were active Facebook users, had Facebook accounts, or how often they used Facebook. Asking nonusers or infrequent users to judge Facebook’s affordances would undermine construct validity of perceived Facebook expression, connection, disclosure safety, and disclosure advantages.
issues.quote: "Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US"; "Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers"

issues.subcategory: perceived affordances treated as actual benefits or behavior
issues.description: The measures assess perceptions that Facebook enables expression, connection, safety, and advantage; they do not measure actual self-disclosure behavior, actual connection, actual social support, or actual psychological benefits. Several interpretations slide from perceived affordances to real benefits or behavioral tendencies.
issues.quote: "Three items each assessed the degree to which participants believed Facebook enabled them to express themselves and to connect with others."; "Our meta-analysis confirmed the original study’s findings that when compared with individuals high in self-esteem, those with low self-esteem saw Facebook as a safer and more advantageous way of self-disclosing relative to FTF interactions."

issues.description: The abstract and discussion state that self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression and that all confidence intervals included zero. However, the results report a statistically significant meta-analytic effect with a confidence/prediction interval from .01 to .14. This is an internal statistical contradiction and changes the interpretation of the outcome.
issues.quote: "self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero)"; "the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero, and the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14"

issues.subcategory: incorrect significance statement for connection effect
issues.description: The results report the meta-analytic connection effect as p = .065 with a 95% CI including zero, but the discussion says it was significantly different from zero. This is a direct statistical error.
issues.quote: "The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065."; "However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero."

issues.description: The fail-safe number for the self-expression analysis is reported as 3 in the results and 5 in the discussion. This inconsistency undermines confidence in the reported robustness statistics.
issues.quote: "The FSN was 3 studies."; "The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant"

issues.description: The fail-safe number for the connection analysis is reported as 5 in the results and 11 in the discussion. This inconsistency affects the interpretation of stability or robustness.
issues.quote: "The FSN was 5 studies."; "These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies)."

issues.subcategory: prediction interval mislabeled for safety effect
issues.description: The results distinguish the safety effect confidence interval from the prediction interval, but the discussion reports the confidence interval as if it were the prediction interval. This changes the expected range for future effects and overstates precision.
issues.quote: "The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was -.28, 95% CI [-.40, -.15], 95% PI [-.54, -.03], p < .001."; "The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well."

issues.description: The connection prediction interval differs between the results and discussion. Although numerically small, it reflects inconsistent reporting of a key inferential statistic.

The original advantageous-disclosure effect is reported inconsistently as -.30, -.33, and beta = -.300. Because the meta-analysis compares replication effects with original effects, inconsistent original effect-size extraction directly affects conclusions about replication success and effect-size differences.
issues.quote: "meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30"; "The effect sizes of all studies were descriptively less than or equal to the original (-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33)"; "Original r | -0.33"; "β | -.300"

issues.description: The manuscript appears to meta-analyze raw correlations directly and states that rma accepts effect size r and N parameters. Correlations should generally be Fisher-z transformed and analyzed with appropriate sampling variances before back-transformation. The reporting does not specify such transformation or variance calculation, making the meta-analytic estimates and intervals difficult to evaluate.
issues.quote: "The rma function was used, which accepts the effect size r and N parameters"; "Effect size r represented the size and direction of the relationship of self-esteem scores to the four outcome variables"

issues.description: The authors compared REML and DerSimonian-Laird and selected REML because it produced more interpretable estimates. Without a preregistered meta-analytic plan, choosing the estimator after inspecting the data introduces analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: "We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data"

issues.description: The manuscript reports preregistration for individual replications but does not state that the meta-analysis inclusion criteria, extraction decisions, estimator choice, transformations, heterogeneity handling, or robustness analyses were preregistered. This leaves important researcher degrees of freedom undisclosed.
issues.quote: "the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study’s OSF page"; "This meta-analysis synthesized seven direct pre-registered replications"

issues.subcategory: non-independence of effect sizes by institution/team
issues.description: The seven effects are treated as independent, but they come from only five institutions, with repeated studies from the same institution and, in at least one case, the same author group. Unmodeled clustering can underestimate uncertainty and overstate precision in a random-effects meta-analysis.
issues.quote: "seven direct pre-registered replications"; "Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US"; "IIT-Sp16 | Legate, et al."; "IIT-Sp17 | Legate, et al."

issues.description: Four related outcomes are tested separately, and replication conclusions rely partly on p-values, including a small p-value for self-expression. The manuscript does not discuss multiplicity or control of Type I error across outcomes.
issues.quote: "For each of the four outcome variables, we present the standardized beta and p-value for the regressions."

issues.description: The claim that p-values between .04 and .05 are more likely under the true null than under the alternative is not generally valid without assumptions about priors, power, and the distribution of true effects; it also risks overinterpreting a single p-value from the original study.
issues.quote: "p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one"

issues.description: The fail-safe N is described as a method for determining how many unpublished nonsignificant studies would reduce a significant result to nonsignificance, but it is also discussed for a nonsignificant connection meta-analysis and used to support claims about lack of effect. Fail-safe N is not evidence for the null and is generally a weak publication-bias diagnostic, especially with a small set of preregistered replications.
issues.quote: "The FSN analysis was intended to identify the number of non-significant, unreported studies required to add to the meta-analysis to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to non-significance."; "The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065."; "These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN"

issues.subcategory: publication bias inferred from replication-original differences
issues.description: The discussion infers publication bias in the original study from smaller replication effects and prediction intervals. A single original study compared with later replications cannot establish publication bias; differences could reflect sampling error, population change, procedural variation, measurement changes, or platform changes.
issues.quote: "all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study"

issues.description: The manuscript interprets nonsignificant Q tests as little or no heterogeneity even when I2 confidence intervals are extremely wide. With only seven studies, Q has low power and heterogeneity estimates are imprecise, so statements that heterogeneity did not appear present are too strong.
issues.quote: "The between-study variance in the replication studies did not appear to be heterogenous, Q(df = 6) = 4.75, p = .576; T2 = 0, 95% CI [0, .03]; I2 = 0%, 95% CI [0%, 79%]."

issues.description: Prediction intervals estimate the plausible distribution of true effects in a new comparable setting, not that observed effect sizes in 95% of future studies will necessarily fall in the interval. The manuscript repeatedly phrases prediction intervals as direct forecasts of future study findings.
issues.quote: "the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14"; "The 95% PI [-.24, -.08] indicated that future studies are likely to find such an effect."

issues.description: The studies are cross-sectional self-report surveys. Although regression terminology uses 'predictor,' the manuscript makes forward-looking claims about what low-self-esteem individuals will feel or do. Such claims should be framed as associations, not causal or temporal prediction.
issues.quote: "we can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions"

issues.description: Associations between self-esteem and Facebook perceptions may be confounded by Facebook use frequency, social anxiety, extraversion, depressive symptoms, gender, age, cohort, institution, and platform preference. The analyses appear to be simple bivariate regressions and do not address these confounds, limiting interpretation.
issues.quote: "Effect size r represented the size and direction of the relationship of self-esteem scores to the four outcome variables"; "self-esteem was a significant predictor of perceptions"

issues.description: The manuscript motivates the work by reference to Facebook’s global user base, but all participants were U.S. undergraduates, disproportionately female, and only some studies collected race. Claims about Facebook users broadly or worldwide are therefore overgeneralized.
issues.quote: "some two billion people worldwide, including 70% of the U.S. population"; "Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US"; "Across datasets, 67% of all participants were female and 33% were male"

issues.description: Race was collected in only three replications and other demographics were not collected. This prevents assessment of sample comparability, demographic moderation, and representativeness.
issues.quote: "In three replications (BYU-Wi17, IIT-Sp16, and IIT-Sp17), race data was collected, but in all other studies no other demographic information was collected"

issues.subcategory: mode and setting moderators not modeled
issues.description: The studies varied by online versus lab administration, group versus individual completion, wording, scales, and extra measures, but these differences were not modeled. Pooling across heterogeneous methods without planned moderator tests makes it unclear whether between-study differences reflect substantive replication failure or procedural artifacts.
issues.quote: "Because each of these potential moderating factors occurred in only one or two of the seven replications, we chose not to explore these issues in more depth."

issues.description: The study does not measure compensation motives, anxiety in face-to-face interaction, actual online interaction, or social outcomes. Therefore the results provide at most indirect evidence relevant to social compensation theory, yet the manuscript claims support for the theory.
issues.quote: "The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory"

issues.description: The original study and replications occurred in different social-media eras. Facebook’s meaning and use among college students likely changed between the original and 2016–2017 replications. This threatens construct equivalence: a 'direct' Facebook replication may not measure the same social context or affordance perceptions.
issues.quote: "Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others, whereas these platforms would not have been a consideration for participants in Forest and Wood’s (2012) study."

issues.subcategory: ambiguous or inconsistent effect-size difference sign
issues.description: Table 3 does not clearly define the direction of the 'Difference' column, and the signs appear to be original minus replication rather than replication minus original. This ambiguity complicates interpretation of whether replication effects are larger or smaller than original effects.

One replication administered questionnaires to groups of two to six, unlike others where participants completed alone. For measures concerning self-disclosure, social connection, and safety, reduced privacy or peer presence could influence responses.
issues.quote: "Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six."

issues.subcategory: scale wording and response format changes
issues.description: Changing Rosenberg Self-Esteem item wording, order, and response scale may alter the self-esteem construct or score distribution across studies. Although standardization reduces scale-unit differences, wording and format changes can affect reliability and correlations.
issues.quote: "one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items"; "most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale"

issues.subcategory: search and screening procedure for meta-analysis incomplete
issues.description: The meta-analysis is limited to CREP OSF projects, but the manuscript does not provide a systematic search strategy, retrieval date, screening flow, exclusion reasons for nonincluded forks, or whether non-CREP replications existed. This limits reproducibility and risks biased inclusion.
issues.quote: "retrieved from CREP contributions with published data and/or results on the CREP project pages"; "All seven studies were included in this meta-analysis."

issues.subcategory: direct-replication claim inconsistent with acknowledged deviations
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly says all studies were direct replications and that materials and methods were very close to the original, but it later describes substantial variations in mode, setting, scales, wording, scoring, and additional measures. This weakens the conceptual claim that all studies estimate the same direct-replication effect.
issues.quote: "All studies reported in this research were direct replications of the original."; "As the original research did not specify whether participants completed questionnaires in a lab or online, researchers employed both methods"; "Two other known differences across replications involved minor discrepancies in presentation of the RSE scale"
